items.prompt: Define an entrepreneur.
items.canonical_answer: An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a business opportunity and takes the risk of starting and running a business, organising the workers, premises, equipment and money it needs, in the hope of earning profit.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include the taking of risk in starting and running a business; naming a famous founder is not a definition.

items.prompt: Explain why the willingness to take risks is an important characteristic for an entrepreneur.
items.canonical_answer: Starting a business exposes the founder's money and time to loss, because a new business may fail however carefully it is planned; a person unwilling to risk that loss never opens the doors, and the profit the idea might earn never gets its chance. Entrepreneurs who take calculated risks reduce the danger - checking that customers want the product before committing - so the willingness to take risks, tempered by research, is what turns an idea into a trading business.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for identifying that starting a business puts money and time at risk, because success is not certain. Second reason: award for linking risk-taking to the reward of profit, because without the willingness to start, the business never opens.

items.prompt: Explain the features that successful entrepreneurs tend to share.
items.canonical_answer: Successful entrepreneurs tend to share a cluster of characteristics. They work hard, because a young business demands long hours with nobody else to carry the work. They are creative, spotting wants others walk past. They take calculated risks, checking the market before committing money. They are optimistic and self-confident, because a founder who expects failure tends to stop trying. And they communicate well, able to persuade customers, suppliers and a lender to listen. What the list includes above all is tendencies, not promises: the characteristics raise the odds of success, and the surroundings - demand, competition, timing - count alongside the person.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element stated - hard work, creativity, calculated risk-taking, optimism, self-confidence, communication - developed with what each contributes; award for noting these are tendencies rather than a promise of success.

items.prompt: Define a business plan.
items.canonical_answer: A business plan is a written document setting out a business idea, the people behind it, its objectives, its market, its operations and its financial forecasts, usually written before the business starts trading.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include that it is a written document and name at least the objectives, market and financial forecasts; "plans for the business" is not precise enough.

items.prompt: Explain why producing a business plan can save an entrepreneur from an expensive mistake.
items.canonical_answer: Writing the plan forces the founder to research the idea before money is committed: who will buy, at what price, and whether the forecast costs leave anything behind. Weak ideas are often exposed on paper, because the plan puts the revenue and cost forecasts side by side where the gap is visible, so the founder can walk away having spent days rather than savings. The plan then keeps protecting the business after opening, because it sets targets that make weak sales visible early rather than after the money is gone.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the plan testing the idea on paper before money is committed, because the forecasts expose weakness while it is still cheap to walk away. Second reason: award for the plan as a benchmark that surfaces problems early.

items.prompt: Explain the elements a business plan usually contains.
items.canonical_answer: The usual elements are: a description of the product or service; the entrepreneur's details and the team involved; the aims the business will chase; a marketing plan naming target customers and how they will be reached; an operations plan covering premises, equipment and suppliers; and financial forecasts of revenue, start-up costs and likely profit. What a strong plan includes beyond these is the competition the business faces and the risks the founder can foresee, because a plan that ignores its rivals flatters the forecasts it rests on.
marking_guidance: Elements: award for each part - product description, people, aims, marketing plan, operations plan, financial forecasts - and award for what the extras include: competition and foreseeable risks.

items.prompt: A government offers free training courses in costing, pricing and record-keeping to new businesses in a region with high unemployment. Explain how this support could lead to more successful start-ups in the region.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: where start-up founders lack costing and marketing skills, the training fills the gap at no cost to them. Mechanism: trained founders price to cover costs, keep records that surface problems early and market with a purpose, because the courses teach the skills the region's founders most often lack. Consequence: fewer start-ups fail in their first years; the businesses that survive keep trading, so the jobs, incomes and tax the government wants from the scheme stay in the region. The effect is not automatic - training takes time a struggling founder also needs - so it works best for start-ups early enough in their planning to absorb the time cost.
marking_guidance: Condition: award for tying the mechanism to the given starting point - unskilled founders in a high-unemployment region. Mechanism: award for the how - training improves pricing, records and marketing, because those skills keep costs and sales visible. Consequence: award for the effect on the start-ups and the regional economy, the stakeholder the scheme serves. Objective: award for linking back to the government's aim - jobs and economic activity.

items.prompt: Selma's tailoring workshop in Otjiwarongo has four machines and one skilled assistant. She can accept an equipment grant of N$15 000 or a free six-month training scheme covering costing, pricing and record-keeping, but not both this year. Explain what Selma should consider before choosing.
items.canonical_answer: The context here: four machines, one skilled assistant, and a one-time choice between grant and training. The reasoning turns on her binding constraint. If orders are waiting while machines sit idle, machines are the constraint, so the grant buys capacity and is the better tool. If prices are guessed and costs unrecorded, skill is the constraint, because new machines would stand idle while the workshop's pricing stays weak - the training lifts the whole operation. The choice also has a time cost: training takes months the workshop must survive. Conclusion: Selma should first work out where her bottleneck bites - capacity or skill - and take the grant if orders already exceed what four machines can sew, the training if weak costing and records are what hold the business back.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named facts - four machines, one assistant, the one-time choice. Reasoning: award for linking the choice to her binding constraint, because the value of each option depends on where the bottleneck is. Conclusion: award for a justified choice for this workshop.

items.prompt: Explain the main forms of government support available to a business start-up.
items.canonical_answer: The main forms are: grants - money given for a purpose such as equipment or training, not repaid; training schemes - short courses in costing, marketing, record-keeping or the technical skills of the trade; cheap premises in government small-business centres; and advisory services that pair a founder with someone who has run a business before. What the forms share is their target: the cost of getting going and the skills the founder lacks, because those are the two barriers a start-up faces hardest. The support is usually conditional - on location, sector or purpose - so a founder reads the conditions before counting on it.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "When a government gives a start-up a grant, the government becomes involved in running that business." Explain why this statement is wrong.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing support with ownership. In fact, a grant is money given for a purpose the start-up itself carries out: the state takes no shares, appoints no managers and claims none of the profit, so decisions and earnings stay entirely with the entrepreneur - Selma keeps every choice of her workshop and every dollar it makes. Involvement in running a company is a different arrangement altogether, where the state owns or directs an enterprise itself. The test that tells the pair apart: ask who owns the assets and who makes the daily decisions. If both answers point to the entrepreneur, the government is a supporter standing outside the business, not an operator inside it.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact support and running the business are different arrangements - award for that correction. Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair: ownership and day-to-day control.

items.prompt: Define capital employed.
items.canonical_answer: Capital employed is the total money invested in a business's assets - its buildings, vehicles, machinery and equipment - used as one way of measuring how big a business is. Here 'capital' means invested money, not the capital goods of Topic 1.1.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must tie capital employed to money invested in the business's assets and state the sense of 'capital' used; "money the business has" is not precise.

items.prompt: Explain the benefit of measuring business size by the value of output rather than by the number of people employed.
items.canonical_answer: Value of output captures what a business actually produces in money terms, so it can compare firms whose production methods differ: an automated bottler with a dozen workers can out-produce a hand workshop of sixty, and the output measure shows the truth of that, because it values production rather than headcount. The benefit leads to fairer comparisons between capital-intensive and labour-intensive firms, which the employment count alone would rank backwards.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for output valuing production across different methods, developed because headcount hides automation, which leads to fairer comparison between firms with different production methods.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of using the number of people employed to measure business size.
items.canonical_answer: The employment count ignores how a business produces. Two firms can employ the same number of people yet differ enormously in what they make: a modern bottling line employs few people and produces enormous value, while a hand-finishing workshop employs many and produces less, so the employment figure points the wrong way when the two are compared. Because the measure also ignores whether staff are part-time or full-time, it can mislead about which business is really bigger.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the weakness identified - it ignores production methods and hours - developed because two firms with equal headcount can produce very different value, which leads to misleading rankings.

items.prompt: Oshakati Bread employs 40 people, sells bread worth N$6 million a year and has capital employed of N$4 million. Windhoek Precision Tools employs 15 people, produces output worth N$8 million and has capital employed of N$11 million. Using these figures, explain which business you would call the bigger, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The figures give three different answers. By people employed, Oshakati Bread is bigger: 40 against 15. By value of output, the toolmaker leads: N$8 million against N$6 million. By capital employed, the toolmaker is far ahead: N$11 million against N$4 million. The reasoning: because the measures disagree, any verdict must name the measure it uses - the toolmaker's few staff work with heavy machines, which is why it leads on output and capital but not on employment. Conclusion: on two of the three measures the toolmaker is the bigger business, so that is the verdict I would give, while noting the bakery is the bigger employer - the choice of measure is itself part of the answer.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named figures in each pairing - 40 against 15, N$8 million against N$6 million, N$11 million against N$4 million. Reasoning: award for the link between the disagreement of the measures and the need to name one. Conclusion: award for a justified verdict for these two businesses.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the three methods of measuring business size.
items.canonical_answer: The three methods are: the number of people employed - a headcount of the workforce; the value of output - what the business's production is worth over a period, in N$; and capital employed - the money invested in the business's assets, in N$. What each includes is a different dimension of size: labour, production and investment. Profit is not among them: profit measures how well a business is doing rather than how big it is, so a large firm can be loss-making and a small one profitable.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each of the three elements - people employed, value of output, capital employed - with what each captures, and award for the note that profit is not a size measure.

items.prompt: Explain the benefit to an analyst of knowing the limitations of the three size measures.
items.canonical_answer: Knowing the limitations tells the analyst exactly where each measure can mislead: employment hides automation, output value swells with bought-in materials, and capital employed depends on the trade. The benefit is better judgement, because the analyst compares several measures instead of trusting one number - a single figure is evidence rather than a verdict - which leads to a fairer, better-supported conclusion about which business is bigger.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the analyst being warned where each measure misleads, developed because each weakness has a known cause in how businesses differ, which leads to using several measures together.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of judging business size from a single measure on its own.
items.canonical_answer: A single measure can rank two businesses the wrong way round. A car dealer reselling vehicles may report output worth N$20 million from a small staff, while a repair garage employing more people reports far less: on output value alone the dealer looks much the bigger, but much of that value belongs to the makers whose cars it passes on, so the ranking misleads about the garage's real activity. Used alone, one measure hides what the others would have shown, because each sees only one dimension of size.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the misleading ranking, developed because bought-in materials inflate output value, which leads to a verdict another measure would reverse.

items.canonical_answer: What the limitations include, measure by measure: for employment, it ignores how the business produces and the mix of part-time and full-time staff, because an automated firm makes more with fewer hands; for value of output, it swells with bought-in materials, because a reseller's sales include the whole value of what it passes on; for capital employed, it depends on the trade, because a haulier's fleet costs a fortune while a design studio needs little more than laptops. items.prompt: The owners of a successful single-outlet bakery want to expand to a second and third outlet. Explain how this expansion could lead to higher profit for the owners, and what could go wrong on the way.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if the bakery's bread sells in the new outlets the way it sells now, expansion changes the business's scale. Mechanism: more outlets raise total sales, and fixed costs such as the head baker's salary and the delivery van spread across more loaves, so internal economies of scale - bulk flour discounts among them - tend to lower the cost per loaf up to a point; provided the new outlets keep the old standards, the margin on each extra loaf reaches the owners as profit. Consequence: total profit and market share rise together. What could go wrong: past the point the owners can supervise, coordination thins and diseconomies raise costs again; the second outlet may be sited badly and drain money before it earns; and a profitable business can still run short of cash while the fittings are being paid for, because profit and cash are not the same thing - the spending lands before the earning. For the owners as the stakeholders, profit rises only while the extra revenue outruns the extra costs.
marking_guidance: Condition: award for tying the chain to the given starting point - a successful bakery adding outlets. Mechanism: award for the how - fixed costs spread and bulk discounts arrive, because scale lowers cost per loaf up to a point. Consequence: award for the effect on the owners' profit and the business's market share. Objective: award for the owners as the stakeholder whose profit the expansion serves, and for the risks that can reverse it.

items.prompt: Maria runs Okahandja Party Tents, hiring out marquees from one yard she controls herself. A rival's closure has left demand she cannot meet, and expanding would mean a second depot, a bank loan and a hired manager. Explain what expanding would give Maria and what it would cost her, and what her final decision should rest on.
items.canonical_answer: The context: unmet demand since the rival closed, a loan and a hired manager if she expands, and total control if she does not. The reasoning: expanding would bring the extra revenue and market share the rival left behind, because the demand is there now; but the loan must be serviced in a weak season as much as a strong one, and control would pass partly to a manager - the personal attention she built the name on would dilute. Expansion is also no promise of more profit: the second depot must be stocked and staffed long before it earns. Conclusion: her decision should rest on her own objective. If she prizes control and a modest, reliable income, staying near her current size is the rational choice; if she wants growth in profit, she should expand provided the loan terms leave room for a bad season.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named facts - unmet demand, loan, manager, personal control. Reasoning: award for linking each side to her objectives, because expansion serves profit while control serves other aims. Conclusion: award for a choice conditional on her own objective.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main reasons owners have for wanting to expand their businesses.
items.canonical_answer: The main reasons include: higher profit, because more sales tend to leave more over provided costs behave; a larger market share, which weakens rivals and strengthens the business's hand with suppliers; lower unit costs, because fixed costs spread over more output up to a point, past which diseconomies begin to push costs back up; reduced risk, because selling to more markets means a downturn in one does not sink the whole business; and personal status and satisfaction, because many owners take pride in a growing name and the jobs it creates. What the list includes underneath is a set of hopes, not results - the motive is not the outcome, and each owner weighs gain against cost and risk differently.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - profit, market share, unit costs, risk-spreading, status - with what it includes, and award for noting these are hoped-for outcomes rather than results.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Expanding a business always increases its profit, because a bigger business earns more than a small one." Explain why this reasoning is wrong.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is treating expansion and rising profit as the same thing. In fact, expansion is a change in the scale of operations, while profit is what remains after every cost is paid: the second outlet must be fitted out, staffed and stocked long before it earns, so a growing business can be busier and poorer at once, and a badly chosen site can lose money for years. Growth and profit are linked only when the extra revenue outruns the extra costs - which is a condition, not a rule. The test that tells the pair apart: ask whether the statement is about the size of operations or about the money left over after costs. Expansion changes the first; only the costs and revenues together decide the second.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact expansion changes scale, not profit directly - award for that correction. Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair: scale of operations against what remains after costs.

items.prompt: Define internal growth.
items.canonical_answer: Internal growth - also called organic growth - is expansion achieved with the business's own resources, such as opening new outlets, extending the product range or winning more customers, without joining with another business. External growth, by contrast, expands the business through a merger or a takeover.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include the business's own resources and no other business joining; contrasting it with external growth shows the boundary.

items.prompt: Explain the benefit to a business's owners of internal growth compared with external growth.
items.canonical_answer: Internal growth keeps ownership and control exactly where they were: no new owners arrive, so the founders' strategy is not diluted by merger partners, and the business expands only as fast as its people and systems can absorb. The pace also protects what exists, because each step - a new outlet, an extended range - is funded and proven before the next is taken, which leads to growth the owners still recognise and direct rather than growth they must negotiate with someone else.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for control staying with the owners, developed because no new owners or partners arrive, which leads to expansion paced to what the business can absorb.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of internal growth as a way of expanding a business.
items.canonical_answer: Internal growth is slow. Building a second outlet, a new product line and a wider customer base from the business's own resources takes years, because the money for each step must be earned or borrowed and each step must prove itself before the next. Meanwhile rivals can grow externally overnight: a competitor that buys an established chain starts with its branches, trained staff and customers already working, so a business that relies on internal growth can find its market taken while it builds.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the slowness, developed because each step must be financed and proven, which leads to the risk that faster rivals take the market first.

items.prompt: Rundu Family Bakery runs one shop and wants to grow. Option A is a second shop of her own: about N$220 000 of equipment and building work, expected to add sales of around N$340 000 a year, starting with no customers. Option B is taking over a struggling competitor for about N$400 000, bringing its equipment, trained staff and customers from day one. Using the figures, explain what the owner should weigh in choosing between internal and external growth.
items.canonical_answer: The facts: internal growth here costs about N$220 000 and builds sales of around N$340 000 a year from nothing, while external growth costs about N$400 000 and buys an operating trade - a takeover, so its staff and customers arrive at once. The reasoning: the takeover buys speed and proven demand, because the competitor already trades; but it costs about N$180 000 more and leaves two ways of working to merge, which is where takeovers most often go wrong. The second shop is cheaper and keeps every decision with the owner, but its N$340 000 of expected sales must be built customer by customer. Conclusion: if the owner's cash can carry the larger loan and she is confident of merging the two teams, the takeover is likely to pay sooner because its customers already exist; if not, the second shop is the safer internal route.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Kavango Timber Mills is a bigger business than its rival because it has more working capital." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing working capital with capital employed. Capital employed is the total money invested in a business's assets - for a timber mill, its saws, kilns, trucks and buildings - and it is one of the accepted measures of business size, alongside the number of people employed and the value of output. Working capital is a different figure: current assets such as cash, inventory and money owed by customers, minus current liabilities such as bills due to suppliers in the near future. It describes the short-term money available to run the business day to day, not how big the business is. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the figure counts the long-term investment in what the business has built, or the short-term pool left to pay the next bills. The first can measure size; the second cannot. A smaller rival can hold more working capital simply because a large customer has just paid, so the learner's comparison shows which mill has more ready money at that moment. To compare size, the learner should compare capital employed, people employed or value of output.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact the learner has used working capital, a short-term measure of the money available to run the business day to day, where a measure of size such as capital employed is needed.

A 6-mark answer states what capital employed measures (money invested in the business's assets, one measure of size), states what working capital measures (current assets minus current liabilities), and gives the test that separates them - long-term investment against the short-term pool - applied to the two mills.

items.prompt: Andes Wool Workshop is a three-year-old weaving business in Cusco, Peru, with eleven weavers selling blankets to tourists and one hotel. A regional development agency offers free places on a costing and marketing course, and a larger textile firm has proposed a takeover that would keep the weavers employed but end the owners' control. The owners want the workshop to stay part of the community. Analyse the position and recommend what Andes Wool Workshop should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the workshop's constraints are skills and market reach rather than looms - it sells to walk-in tourists and a single hotel, so its prices and its customer list are what hold back the income its eleven weavers could earn. The agency course is support without ownership: it addresses costing and marketing while every decision and every profit stays with the owners, which fits their stated aim of keeping the workshop part of the community. The takeover is external growth by another name: it brings the larger firm's finance and distribution at speed, but control leaves, because a takeover means the buyer decides. Staying small is here a chosen position with a market - tourists and one hotel - that currently supports eleven weavers; whether it stays a success depends on whether that market can be widened without widening the ownership. Recommendation: take the training and keep independence, growing internally into more hotel contracts as demand proves itself; consider the takeover only if community control were protected in writing, which a full takeover is unlikely to offer. The counterargument weighs honestly: the larger firm's reach could secure volume and steadier wages the workshop cannot reach alone. The judgement rests on the criterion the question itself supplies - fit with the owners' objective - and the recommendation depends on the market absorbing modest growth and the owners finding the course time.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation. Context: award for using the facts of the workshop - eleven weavers, tourists and one hotel, agency course, takeover offer, the owners' stated aim. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - fit with the owners' objective of community control. Counterargument: award for the case for the takeover - reach, volume, steadier wages. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on market demand and the training time.
